**Euclid** (; Ancient Greek: Εὐκλείδης; fl.300 BC) was an ancient Greek mathematician active as a geometer and logician.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclid#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBruno2003[httpsarchiveorgdetailsmathmathematicia00brunpage125_125]-2) Considered the "father of geometry",[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclid#cite_note-FOOTNOTESialaros2021%C2%A7_%22Summary%22-3) he is chiefly known for the _[Elements](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclid's\_Elements "Euclid's Elements")_ treatise, which established the foundations of geometry that largely dominated the field until the early 19th century. His system, now referred to as Euclidean geometry, involved innovations in combination with a synthesis of theories from earlier Greek mathematicians, including Eudoxus of Cnidus, Hippocrates of Chios, Thales and Theaetetus. With Archimedes and Apollonius of Perga, Euclid is generally considered among the greatest mathematicians of antiquity, and one of the most influential in the history of mathematics.

Very little is known of Euclid's life, and most information comes from the scholars Proclus and Pappus of Alexandria many centuries later. Medieval Islamic mathematicians invented a fanciful biography, and medieval Byzantine and early Renaissance scholars mistook him for the earlier philosopher Euclid of Megara. It is now generally accepted that he spent his career in Alexandria and lived around 300 BC, after Plato's students and before Archimedes. There is some speculation that Euclid studied at the Platonic Academy and later taught at the Musaeum; he is regarded as bridging the earlier Platonic tradition in Athens with the later tradition of Alexandria.
In the _Elements_, Euclid deduced the theorems from a small set of axioms. He also wrote works on perspective, conic sections, spherical geometry, number theory, and mathematical rigour. In addition to the _Elements_, Euclid wrote a central early text in the optics field, _[Optics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclid's\_Optics "Euclid's Optics")_, and lesser-known works including _[Data](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclid's\_Data "Euclid's Data")_ and _Phaenomena_. Euclid's authorship of _On Divisions of Figures_ and _Catoptrics_ has been questioned. He is thought to have written many lost works.

The English name 'Euclid' is the anglicized version of the Ancient Greek name _Eukleídes_ (Εὐκλείδης).[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclid#cite_note-FOOTNOTESialaros2021%C2%A7_%22Life%22-4)[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclid#cite_note-6) It is derived from 'eu-' (εὖ; 'well'), 'klês' (-κλῆς; 'fame'), meaning "renowned, glorious",[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclid#cite_note-FOOTNOTE''OED''b-7) and the suffix '-ides' (-ίδης, 'son of'). In English, by metonymy, 'Euclid' can mean his most well-known work, [Euclid's _Elements_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclid's_Elements "Euclid's Elements"), or a copy thereof,[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclid#cite_note-FOOTNOTE''OED''a-5) and is sometimes synonymous with 'geometry'.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclid#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBruno2003[httpsarchiveorgdetailsmathmathematicia00brunpage125_125]-2)

Euclid is called the father of geometry because he basically created the geometry that people do today. In his book "Elements," Euclid gathered up all of the known mathematics of his time, as well as a lot of his own, and then he subjected it all to logical, mathematic proofs. ### Who is Euclid and why is he important to mathematics?
##### Recommended lessons and courses for you
Euclid's _Elements_ is a thirteen-volume text that compiled everything known about mathematics in Euclid's time, gathering and summing up the work of Pythagoras, Hippocrates, Theudius, Theaetetus, and Eudoxus. Adding his own work to the mix, Euclid compiled all of this existing mathematical knowledge into a contiguous, complete framework. Most importantly, Euclid introduced the form for logic-based **mathematical proofs**, where **theorems** are built from known, true statements called **axioms**. For all of the mathematics presented in _Elements,_ Euclid worked from a base of five geometric axioms and five mathematical axioms, and all geometry was constructed with only a straightedge and a compass. Euclid's work with plane geometry was so comprehensive and influential that today it is called **Euclidian Geometry**. Any sort of non-Euclidian geometry (geometry on a curved surface, for instance) did not fully emerge until the 19th Century.
Which Greek mathematician is known as the father of geometry? That would be Euclid, also called the founder of geometry. Mathematicians referred to Euclid in their own works for millennia after his death, but his books were not only known in mathematics circles, so to speak. _Elements_ earned renown as a text for logic and reason as well. George Washington and Thomas Jefferson both referred to Euclid for his logical reasoning (though Jefferson did to essentially defend the practice of slavery). Abraham Lincoln carried a copy of _Elements_ with him for much of his adult life and at one point he dedicated himself to mastering the first six books. Albert Einstein described the _Elements_ as "a wonder." "If Euclid failed to kindle your youthful enthusiasm," Einstein wrote, "then you were not born to be a scientific thinker."

### Who is Euclid and why is he important to mathematics?
##### Recommended lessons and courses for you
**Euclid** was a Greek mathematician who wrote the book**_Elements_**, which is regarded as one of the most important math books to exist. Euclid was born around 325 BC. He moved to Alexandria, Egypt at an early age and he spent most of his life there. Historical accounts claim that he studied under Plato's philosophy and that he was a generally fair and helpful teacher to his students later in life. Beyond that, few details of Euclid's life are known. Euclid wrote a number of mathematical volumes in his career, but by far the most influential was his book _Elements._ The multivolume tome set out the discipline of plane geometry so well that it is known today as **Euclidian Geometry**, and Euclid himself is known as "the father of geometry."
In _Elements_, Euclid established a method for logical **mathematic proofs**, whereby one could show a statement to be true using a series of steps. Euclid's logic was based on starting from **axioms**, statements that are so evident that they must be true, and then building them up into **theorems**, statements that are proved true with reasoning. Throughout _Element's_ thirteen volumes, Euclid worked from a set of 5 mathematical axioms and 5 geometrical axioms, and he showed that all geometry can be drawn with a straightedge and a compass. Euclid proved theorems in geometry, collected all of the known mathematics in his day, and worked with prime numbers and number theory. He applied Euclidian geometry to algebra, proving statements such as "a + b + c = c + b + a." Euclid and _Elements_ were so influential that the book was used directly as _the_ primary geometry textbook until the 20th Century. Euclid and his work have been referenced by mathematicians, historians, logicians, and philosophers, among others, over the twenty-three centuries since his death. Today, a lunar crater, a minor planet, and an upcoming space telescope have been named for him.

The Mathematician Euclid [Mathematics History - 6]
Euclid often referred to as the "Father of Geometry", was a Greek mathematician who lived around 300 BCE. He worked in the city of Alexandria during the reign of Ptolemy I Soter (an Egyptian ruler).
Euclid is well known for writing the book Elements, one of the most influential works in the history of mathematics. In this book, he organized mathematical knowledge into a clear system of using definitions, axioms and logical proofs. It covers topics like geometry, number theory and proportions.
His methods of solving problems, by starting with simple truths and coming up with complex ideas, became one of the foundations of modern mathematics today. Euclid’s work shaped geometry for over 2,000 years.
What we study in school as “Euclidean Geometry” is based directly on his ideas.
Although little is known about his personal life, Euclid’s contributions remain essential to mathematics and science as a whole.

### Why is Euclid called the father of geometry?
Euclid is called the father of geometry because he basically created the geometry that people do today. In his book "Elements," Euclid gathered up all of the known mathematics of his time, as well as a lot of his own, and then he subjected it all to logical, mathematic proofs. His proofs were so well-constructed and his work so influential that "Elements" is still in print today.

### Who is Euclid and why is he important to mathematics?
Euclid was a Greek mathematician who lived in the city of Alexandria around 300 BC. He invented the form of mathematical proof that is still used today. With it, he demonstrated what math that existed in his time was true, and he wrote out a number of theorems in plane geometry and number theory. Euclid proved that there are infinite primes, he showed that basically all geometry can be done with a ruler and compass, and he is now known as the "father of geometry."

### Who is Euclid and why is he important to mathematics?
##### Recommended lessons and courses for you
Euclid's _Elements_ is a thirteen-volume text that compiled everything known about mathematics in Euclid's time, gathering and summing up the work of Pythagoras, Hippocrates, Theudius, Theaetetus, and Eudoxus. Adding his own work to the mix, Euclid compiled all of this existing mathematical knowledge into a contiguous, complete framework. Most importantly, Euclid introduced the form for logic-based **mathematical proofs**, where **theorems** are built from known, true statements called **axioms**. For all of the mathematics presented in _Elements,_ Euclid worked from a base of five geometric axioms and five mathematical axioms, and all geometry was constructed with only a straightedge and a compass. Euclid's work with plane geometry was so comprehensive and influential that today it is called **Euclidian Geometry**. Any sort of non-Euclidian geometry (geometry on a curved surface, for instance) did not fully emerge until the 19th Century.
Which Greek mathematician is known as the father of geometry? That would be Euclid, also called the founder of geometry. Mathematicians referred to Euclid in their own works for millennia after his death, but his books were not only known in mathematics circles, so to speak. _Elements_ earned renown as a text for logic and reason as well. George Washington and Thomas Jefferson both referred to Euclid for his logical reasoning (though Jefferson did to essentially defend the practice of slavery). Abraham Lincoln carried a copy of _Elements_ with him for much of his adult life and at one point he dedicated himself to mastering the first six books. Albert Einstein described the _Elements_ as "a wonder." "If Euclid failed to kindle your youthful enthusiasm," Einstein wrote, "then you were not born to be a scientific thinker."

Euclid proved the Pythagorean Theorem by showing that the areas of the smaller squares add to equal the area of the larger square.
What did Euclid do? Using his system of proofs, Euclid proved some well-known items in mathematics, such as the Pythagorean Theorem. He demonstrated how to calculate the volumes of solids, such as cones and pyramids, and described geometric number sequences. Euclid's first theorem introduced the "Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic," which states that all numbers greater than 1 can be written as factors of prime numbers. Euclid's second theorem was that there were infinitely many prime numbers (he was the first to prove it). Euclid defined and described many different kinds of special numbers, including the _Golden Ratio_. Euclid's impact on mathematics today is immeasurable. Not only is much of his work either taught directly to students or referred to by mathematicians, but his logical framework for mathematical proofs is also still used today, mostly as it was in his time.

### Who is Euclid and why is he important to mathematics?
##### Recommended lessons and courses for you
**Euclid** was a Greek mathematician who wrote the book**_Elements_**, which is regarded as one of the most important math books to exist. Euclid was born around 325 BC. He moved to Alexandria, Egypt at an early age and he spent most of his life there. Historical accounts claim that he studied under Plato's philosophy and that he was a generally fair and helpful teacher to his students later in life. Beyond that, few details of Euclid's life are known. Euclid wrote a number of mathematical volumes in his career, but by far the most influential was his book _Elements._ The multivolume tome set out the discipline of plane geometry so well that it is known today as **Euclidian Geometry**, and Euclid himself is known as "the father of geometry."
In _Elements_, Euclid established a method for logical **mathematic proofs**, whereby one could show a statement to be true using a series of steps. Euclid's logic was based on starting from **axioms**, statements that are so evident that they must be true, and then building them up into **theorems**, statements that are proved true with reasoning. Throughout _Element's_ thirteen volumes, Euclid worked from a set of 5 mathematical axioms and 5 geometrical axioms, and he showed that all geometry can be drawn with a straightedge and a compass. Euclid proved theorems in geometry, collected all of the known mathematics in his day, and worked with prime numbers and number theory. He applied Euclidian geometry to algebra, proving statements such as "a + b + c = c + b + a." Euclid and _Elements_ were so influential that the book was used directly as _the_ primary geometry textbook until the 20th Century. Euclid and his work have been referenced by mathematicians, historians, logicians, and philosophers, among others, over the twenty-three centuries since his death. Today, a lunar crater, a minor planet, and an upcoming space telescope have been named for him.

**Euclid** (; Ancient Greek: Εὐκλείδης; fl.300 BC) was an ancient Greek mathematician active as a geometer and logician.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclid#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBruno2003[httpsarchiveorgdetailsmathmathematicia00brunpage125_125]-2) Considered the "father of geometry",[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclid#cite_note-FOOTNOTESialaros2021%C2%A7_%22Summary%22-3) he is chiefly known for the _[Elements](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclid's\_Elements "Euclid's Elements")_ treatise, which established the foundations of geometry that largely dominated the field until the early 19th century. His system, now referred to as Euclidean geometry, involved innovations in combination with a synthesis of theories from earlier Greek mathematicians, including Eudoxus of Cnidus, Hippocrates of Chios, Thales and Theaetetus. With Archimedes and Apollonius of Perga, Euclid is generally considered among the greatest mathematicians of antiquity, and one of the most influential in the history of mathematics.
texts.1:
Very little is known of Euclid's life, and most information comes from the scholars Proclus and Pappus of Alexandria many centuries later. Medieval Islamic mathematicians invented a fanciful biography, and medieval Byzantine and early Renaissance scholars mistook him for the earlier philosopher Euclid of Megara. It is now generally accepted that he spent his career in Alexandria and lived around 300 BC, after Plato's students and before Archimedes. There is some speculation that Euclid studied at the Platonic Academy and later taught at the Musaeum; he is regarded as bridging the earlier Platonic tradition in Athens with the later tradition of Alexandria.
In the _Elements_, Euclid deduced the theorems from a small set of axioms. He also wrote works on perspective, conic sections, spherical geometry, number theory, and mathematical rigour. In addition to the _Elements_, Euclid wrote a central early text in the optics field, _[Optics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclid's\_Optics "Euclid's Optics")_, and lesser-known works including _[Data](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclid's\_Data "Euclid's Data")_ and _Phaenomena_. Euclid's authorship of _On Divisions of Figures_ and _Catoptrics_ has been questioned. He is thought to have written many lost works.

The Mathematician Euclid [Mathematics History - 6]
Euclid often referred to as the "Father of Geometry", was a Greek mathematician who lived around 300 BCE. He worked in the city of Alexandria during the reign of Ptolemy I Soter (an Egyptian ruler).
Euclid is well known for writing the book Elements, one of the most influential works in the history of mathematics. In this book, he organized mathematical knowledge into a clear system of using definitions, axioms and logical proofs. It covers topics like geometry, number theory and proportions.
His methods of solving problems, by starting with simple truths and coming up with complex ideas, became one of the foundations of modern mathematics today. Euclid’s work shaped geometry for over 2,000 years.
What we study in school as “Euclidean Geometry” is based directly on his ideas.
Although little is known about his personal life, Euclid’s contributions remain essential to mathematics and science as a whole.

Euclid's _Elements_ is a thirteen-volume text that compiled everything known about mathematics in Euclid's time, gathering and summing up the work of Pythagoras, Hippocrates, Theudius, Theaetetus, and Eudoxus. Adding his own work to the mix, Euclid compiled all of this existing mathematical knowledge into a contiguous, complete framework. Most importantly, Euclid introduced the form for logic-based **mathematical proofs**, where **theorems** are built from known, true statements called **axioms**. For all of the mathematics presented in _Elements,_ Euclid worked from a base of five geometric axioms and five mathematical axioms, and all geometry was constructed with only a straightedge and a compass. Euclid's work with plane geometry was so comprehensive and influential that today it is called **Euclidian Geometry**. Any sort of non-Euclidian geometry (geometry on a curved surface, for instance) did not fully emerge until the 19th Century.
Which Greek mathematician is known as the father of geometry? That would be Euclid, also called the founder of geometry. Mathematicians referred to Euclid in their own works for millennia after his death, but his books were not only known in mathematics circles, so to speak. _Elements_ earned renown as a text for logic and reason as well. George Washington and Thomas Jefferson both referred to Euclid for his logical reasoning (though Jefferson did to essentially defend the practice of slavery). Abraham Lincoln carried a copy of _Elements_ with him for much of his adult life and at one point he dedicated himself to mastering the first six books. Albert Einstein described the _Elements_ as "a wonder." "If Euclid failed to kindle your youthful enthusiasm," Einstein wrote, "then you were not born to be a scientific thinker."

### Who is Euclid and why is he important to mathematics?
##### Recommended lessons and courses for you
**Euclid** was a Greek mathematician who wrote the book**_Elements_**, which is regarded as one of the most important math books to exist. Euclid was born around 325 BC. He moved to Alexandria, Egypt at an early age and he spent most of his life there. Historical accounts claim that he studied under Plato's philosophy and that he was a generally fair and helpful teacher to his students later in life. Beyond that, few details of Euclid's life are known. Euclid wrote a number of mathematical volumes in his career, but by far the most influential was his book _Elements._ The multivolume tome set out the discipline of plane geometry so well that it is known today as **Euclidian Geometry**, and Euclid himself is known as "the father of geometry."
In _Elements_, Euclid established a method for logical **mathematic proofs**, whereby one could show a statement to be true using a series of steps. Euclid's logic was based on starting from **axioms**, statements that are so evident that they must be true, and then building them up into **theorems**, statements that are proved true with reasoning. Throughout _Element's_ thirteen volumes, Euclid worked from a set of 5 mathematical axioms and 5 geometrical axioms, and he showed that all geometry can be drawn with a straightedge and a compass. Euclid proved theorems in geometry, collected all of the known mathematics in his day, and worked with prime numbers and number theory. He applied Euclidian geometry to algebra, proving statements such as "a + b + c = c + b + a." Euclid and _Elements_ were so influential that the book was used directly as _the_ primary geometry textbook until the 20th Century. Euclid and his work have been referenced by mathematicians, historians, logicians, and philosophers, among others, over the twenty-three centuries since his death. Today, a lunar crater, a minor planet, and an upcoming space telescope have been named for him.

**Euclid** (; Ancient Greek: Εὐκλείδης; fl.300 BC) was an ancient Greek mathematician active as a geometer and logician.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclid#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBruno2003[httpsarchiveorgdetailsmathmathematicia00brunpage125_125]-2) Considered the "father of geometry",[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclid#cite_note-FOOTNOTESialaros2021%C2%A7_%22Summary%22-3) he is chiefly known for the _[Elements](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclid's\_Elements "Euclid's Elements")_ treatise, which established the foundations of geometry that largely dominated the field until the early 19th century. His system, now referred to as Euclidean geometry, involved innovations in combination with a synthesis of theories from earlier Greek mathematicians, including Eudoxus of Cnidus, Hippocrates of Chios, Thales and Theaetetus. With Archimedes and Apollonius of Perga, Euclid is generally considered among the greatest mathematicians of antiquity, and one of the most influential in the history of mathematics.

Very little is known of Euclid's life, and most information comes from the scholars Proclus and Pappus of Alexandria many centuries later. Medieval Islamic mathematicians invented a fanciful biography, and medieval Byzantine and early Renaissance scholars mistook him for the earlier philosopher Euclid of Megara. It is now generally accepted that he spent his career in Alexandria and lived around 300 BC, after Plato's students and before Archimedes. There is some speculation that Euclid studied at the Platonic Academy and later taught at the Musaeum; he is regarded as bridging the earlier Platonic tradition in Athens with the later tradition of Alexandria.
In the _Elements_, Euclid deduced the theorems from a small set of axioms. He also wrote works on perspective, conic sections, spherical geometry, number theory, and mathematical rigour. In addition to the _Elements_, Euclid wrote a central early text in the optics field, _[Optics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclid's\_Optics "Euclid's Optics")_, and lesser-known works including _[Data](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclid's\_Data "Euclid's Data")_ and _Phaenomena_. Euclid's authorship of _On Divisions of Figures_ and _Catoptrics_ has been questioned. He is thought to have written many lost works.

The Mathematician Euclid [Mathematics History - 6]
Euclid often referred to as the "Father of Geometry", was a Greek mathematician who lived around 300 BCE. He worked in the city of Alexandria during the reign of Ptolemy I Soter (an Egyptian ruler).
Euclid is well known for writing the book Elements, one of the most influential works in the history of mathematics. In this book, he organized mathematical knowledge into a clear system of using definitions, axioms and logical proofs. It covers topics like geometry, number theory and proportions.
His methods of solving problems, by starting with simple truths and coming up with complex ideas, became one of the foundations of modern mathematics today. Euclid’s work shaped geometry for over 2,000 years.
What we study in school as “Euclidean Geometry” is based directly on his ideas.
Although little is known about his personal life, Euclid’s contributions remain essential to mathematics and science as a whole.
